comp-m4voj1wh: Fountains are devices that have traditionally played an ornamental role, especially in garden settings. The antejardín —that strip of ground between the street and the house— thus becomes an ambiguous stage: not entirely public, not entirely private. I was drawn to its liminal character, its condition as a threshold, and I wanted to consider what happens when the usual order of the objects that inhabit it is disturbed.

Antejardín explores the functionality —or the lack of it— of the elements that tend to populate this space: tools, containers, shovels, soil, watering cans and fountains. Rather than reproduce their form or their use, I set out to operate on them, to throw them out of true, to let their fragility show through.

Recreating an antejardín therefore became a question about the order of things: a watering can covered in soil, a pair of bent shovels, a fallen planter, a mound of earth with ceramic flowers jutting out, a broken pipe suspended in the air. These ceramic artefacts —watering cans without holes, containers that leak, unfinished fountains— do not seek to resolve a function, but to become questions about it.

These formal and symbolic alterations point to the fragility of the structures that organise the domestic, the decorative, the useful. As in a fountain, water does not always follow the course laid out for it: sometimes it strays, pools, or disappears.

comp-m2c5vnee1: “Bache” is a project that sets out to explore a body of vessels from different periods and cultures. Vessels are, essentially, objects with handles or grips, made to hold and carry their contents. Following that logic: if they have no bottom, have they stopped being vessels?

“Bache” proposes a scene in which the pieces appear to sink, or to have been petrified, through cuts made crosswise at different points on each one. It aims to produce an inconsistency in the notions of completeness and stability. The resulting unevenness, and the material itself, open up a question about the discourses that historically frame these objects, bringing together in a single space a selection of pre-Hispanic clay vessels and Western jugs from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, usually metal or porcelain.
The pieces are made of fine reddish grog clay, which relates to local pottery. This gesture also casts the group of objects as entities that imitate a certain materiality and historicity.

comp-m4wykpt1: VASIJA / VER / VACIAR was a ceramics workshop focused on the study of pre-Hispanic practices and their possible uses in a contemporary context. It took place in Bogotá in 2024 and ran for three months. It was conceived as a space for learning, experimentation and material reflection.

The workshop was run by Materia Prima, an artists’ collective formed by Paloma Pardo and Sofía Lozano. It proposed an approach to various ways of building a vessel, and to specific techniques such as terra sigillata —an ancient ceramic finish that involves applying refined clays to produce polished, smooth, highly detailed surfaces without the need for glazes. This technique made it possible to explore relationships between surface, record and trace, in dialogue with the pre-Hispanic practices addressed in the workshop.

The process grew out of a residency by the artist Sofía Lozano in Ecuador, where she visited collections and museums in Quito, among them the Weilbauer Museum and the National Museum of Ecuador. There she came into contact with practices of conservation, classification and preservation of archaeological pieces, experiences that fed the conceptual and methodological approach of the workshop.

comp-lrec7ek32: In this show, what stands for the body is something that believes it knows itself, yet searches for itself in actions, roles, names, definitions and forms. The body that knows itself inserts itself into places that let it explore through symbols and through experience itself; it operates as an object seeking new meanings, turning around the sense its context dictates to it, and it is precisely in this self-knowing that it steps outside itself and is remade. This piece brings together 50 packaging corners that were “left over” once opened. They sit on a perforated board and recall the panels used in hardware shops to display assorted nuts and small parts.

comp-lrfbm9k4: This work is the record of an action that proposes the word as an element of the landscape in public space. A large sheet of paper draws a thin black margin inside itself; within it one reads dejar que la forma se haga —letting the form happen.
The paper is allowed to be affected by its surroundings: touching the ground, a wall, a pavement, and so taking on different shapes.

It is a sunny day; the shadow cast through the branches and leaves of a tree projects a blurred outline; the cracks and unevenness of the ground produce the same effect on the sheet. It is an urban murmur, an abandoned object.

comp-lrfe02kk3: A signal is a sign, a gesture or some other indication or warning of something. We read signals when we communicate with another person and manage to grasp what that gesture means. Signals may involve devices, flashing lights, movements of the hands, the arms or other parts of the body, and they exist in order to warn, alert or point something out.

In this project we devised signals to serve each day, over the course of three laboratories, building a dialogue out of the materials, the participants, and the situation or subject we set out to explore that day. In this sense we made objects, some of them ephemeral, meant to catch someone’s attention and try to tell them something.

"Señales" took place between 30 November and 7 December 2021 at "Más Allá", in Bogotá and its surroundings. Eight sessions of the three laboratories were held, attended by people curious about exploring, through collective making, ideas around the body, disguise, lightness, and the appearance of an image by means of an analogue printing technique (cyanotype). The photographs shown here are the result of those exercises.

SIGNAL 1. Making things in order to disappear. 30 November - 3 December. SIGNAL 2. Let us play in the forest. 2 and 7 December. SIGNAL 3. Inventory through cyanotype, analogue printing. 1 - 4 December.

comp-lrfdguzt1: nada de lo que se mide es basura
comp-lrfdguzz1: This project explores the standard codes and measurements used in archaeological records, building a narrative out of the question of what deserves to be studied and measured, and so opening up possibilities around subjective interests.

For a month I walked the streets around the La Esmeralda neighbourhood in Bogotá, where I was living at the time, finding fragments of rubber and plastic, parts of accessories, pieces of acrylic. These objects had a history bound directly to the area, which prompted the idea of making a series of drawings in which I could experiment with archaeological codes by designing templates and drawing over them. The exercise leads one to think that whatever is measured and recorded holds material and archaeological value.

In the series "Contacto", pieces I made in clay, I used the clay as a matrix to apply pressure, impressing on it the features, textures, reliefs and contours of these objects that belong to a whole that no longer exists.

comp-lrh7i87c1: “Fragmentos Móviles”. Curated by Andrea Infante and Paula Leuro.
comp-lrh7i87e1: This exhibition is an assembly of moments, encounters with situations and actions that happen out of step with one another. It is the result of what chance makes possible: it is built around a play of language and chance. Its axis is not a theme but an object —a deck of cards. A structure with the finish line up high reveals the course of Estefanía’s decisions. The movement of her body is the starting point for every idea. Awareness of her own axis in space leads her to trace a route along which to move. A garden of petrified animals —toads, turtles and fireflies— in which Daniel sets up a game of reading and narration: the pretext for creating an ecosystem where nature is formed out of industrial elements. A rosary that changes shape to become a plane, each mystery held, found and kept by David. Four pieces that guide the silent reading of two elements. A set of suspended pieces: the play of repetition and suspension of objects is an invention that confronts scale. Archaeological explorations, fossil finds or reinterpretations of them, the trace, the negatives or silhouettes of objects, are the clues for approaching the cartography through which Sofía moves. This exhibition would need only to find a curious eye drawn in by a web of coincidences. An observer amid so much attentive distraction.

comp-lrfbwlei2: This project explores classification, drift and found objects. To carry it out I immersed myself in texts examining collecting through history, and how classifications are bound to a tradition of botanical expeditions. "Linnaeus’s Systema Naturae builds a complete archive gathering the structures of plants and methods for collecting and organising them in herbaria (...) this study of the natural relied not only on export, but also employed various tools such as navigational charts, maps, illustrations and, above all, botanical plates."

Out of this context came the various pieces that make up the project, among them "Mapas Residuales". The work consists of eight large-format drawings in ink on parchment paper. They came from the detailed reproduction of waste I collected over six months. In making new groupings, I decided to establish categories at the very moment of drawing: lines, zeros, the silhouettes of the papers, and so on. The first is the drawing of a crumpled receipt, and I arranged them so as to produce a reading "in layers".

The drawing becomes a tracing. These maps are representations of ideas about a partial perception of space and territory, guided by different interests —economic, political, geographic, topographic. This mobile archive proposes a review from a different angle: not space itself, but what is found within it, elements that happen to mimic the cartographic line.

Some elements can be made out more clearly than others, revealing the many forms they take on after their useful life, which mostly consisted of storing or conveying information. Receipts can be distinguished, scraps of paper with margins, jotted numbers. The drawings are set one behind another, dissolving any frontal reading. Only the first and the last can be seen head-on; the rest, from the sides.
Out of this exercise came another 20 drawings in different formats and 2 intaglios.

comp-lrhwsxav2: Winning project of the “En Blanco” open call
comp-lrhwsxay1: The act of digging names an archaeological procedure: the idea of displacing, taking away, removing. Before that exercise, a study has already been made of the territory and of whether it warrants excavation —whether there are signs that a settlement once stood there (pictograms, monuments). Procedimiento fértil probes and proposes a moment prior to Colombia’s recent history: before drug trafficking, before the constitution, before the military coups and other social movements; before any notion of Nation. And yet the first archaeological excavations in Colombia took place at the beginning of the twentieth century, that is, alongside many of those events. The Earth is therefore the protagonist in our relations of power and dominion, but also in what it means to unearth. In any historical scenario it appears as a motive that generates rootedness, attachment or discord. Making a “hole” or a “transfer” thus dislocates the idea of building, possessing and settling. The site of excavation is the place that holds what later comes to be called heritage. It is where the fragments of a reality lie —too dead to understand, too alive to speculate on and imagine. A pattern (taking the definition from design and psychology) is a factor that recurs and tends to repeat. Here the pattern ends up adopting other forms, and steps outside its original function of establishing a relation to human scale. It is also an excavation without a find, concentrated solely on these gestures of measurement.

comp-lrhvtebq1: Residency at No Lugar, Quito, Ecuador.
comp-lrhvtebs1: Sofía Lozano’s project investigates the past of the Tumaco-La Tolita culture, which occupied the Pacific coast of what we now know as Ecuador and Colombia —specifically from the province of Esmeraldas in Ecuador to the north of Buenaventura in Colombia. Its area of influence extended across a territory of roughly 250,000 square kilometres. The history of Tumaco-La Tolita is the result of a long and complex process of mobility, adaptation, continuation, transformation, exchange and cultural evolution, which could be said to begin around 9000 BC with the presence of the Las Vegas culture, one of the first peoples of the Ecuadorian coast, who lived in small groups moving from place to place in search of food. In this sense it is possible to venture an approach, and to propose an account of doubtful provenance about the origin of the Tumaco-La Tolita culture: the Las Vegas culture is the foundation for the development of the Valdivia culture, the first pottery-making culture of Abya Yala, which was the basis for the Chorrera culture, which later became Jama Coaque, who at their cultural height came to be known as Tumaco-La Tolita. Today we stand far from all that; the colonial present and the AD have left us only with fragments, fictions or memories. We do not really know whether the culture was called Tumaco-La Tolita, Valdivia or Las Vegas; those names relate to the places where pre-colonial remains were looted or found, and they may even be fictions archaeology created to justify its “discoveries”. If we used a GPS as the reference for the site, the culture would have a name in coordinates. Through drawing, Lozano speaks of the fragility of maps, of pre-colonial pieces and fragments, to propose a work that erases borders, unifies the territory and questions the fictitious account of colonial archaeological heritage as being of doubtful provenance. “Heritage” answers to a long protocol of colonial verifications that determine what is exhibited, what is told and what is not. Archaeological pieces can be anachronistic objects that may say a great deal or nothing at all; they belong to one culture or another, but in the end they turn out to belong to our culture and to this time.
This project was developed during the residency at No Lugar, Quito, Ecuador, from 1 to 29 October 2023.

comp-m2c5w6ye: everything that does not fit in a display case
comp-m2c5w6yh1: Display cases are essentially divisions that separate viewers from the objects on show. They protect, they hold at a distance, and they lend an aura of status to what they keep. In museums, cases do not only display objects: they also act as supports for texts —labels, historical context, clarifications. Since La Vitrina is a mobile space for experimentation, it seemed a good opportunity to displace one place into another through its semiotic function.

This project sets out a shelf that appears empty but which, once a label is added, takes on new meaning and, above all, becomes a medium that creates and transmits interpretations. Todo lo que no cabe en una vitrina consists of cut-vinyl text applied to the outside of the glass. The text is based on labels I saw at the National Museum. Going back through photos on my phone, the labels and descriptions that caught my attention went beyond a plain reference to the object (date, year) and were rounded out by a story. They describe, for instance, how a mask formed part of a death ritual, how a tea set reflected a social practice of gift-giving, or how a necklace secured the success of an expedition.

I see these labels as fictions, as a possibility of extending into other stories. The final label therefore combines textual references with invented ones, raising questions about the timeline, the event, the object and the place being alluded to.

comp-mh0tn16s: “Atrapar, calar, tejer mitos”. Curated by Arte Vivo
comp-m7mr6giv: This project grew out of a collaboration with Víctor Otero and his mother, Élida Polo, artisans from the department of Sucre, Colombia, who work with caña flecha basketry.

Medir el aire offers a reflection on the objects used for archaeological measurement, and specifically on the scale bar: an instrument made of alternating black and white squares, placed beside objects to give the viewer a reference for their dimensions.
This object has caught my attention for a long time, and in this project it takes material form at a large scale through basketry. It is also a reflection on the notion of measuring itself.

Suspended from the ceiling, and as its name suggests, Medir el aire —measuring the air— alludes more to a movement than to the measurement of anything tangible. By changing the materiality and the language of this measuring instrument, the project suggests a comment on the apparent objectivity of standard metrics, opening up the possibility of imagining other ways of relating to time, the body, weight and space.

This piece formed part of the exhibition Atrapar, calar, tejer mitos, shown at ARTBO International Fair 2025, at the Claustro de Las Aguas of Artesanías de Colombia, in the exhibition hall of the Faculty of Creation and Communication at Universidad del Rosario, and at Expoartesanías Colombia 2025.
